sources.title: David Eby’s big gamble: Why calling an early B.C. election could backfire

discussion.body: An early election is a timing trade: keep governing into an uncertain stretch, or take the voters now. If the right has held power for roughly six decades of the post-war period and the NDP for about 22 years, choosing your moment is not vanity — it's the whole game.

Treating 'the various parties of the right' as a single bloc across six decades does a lot of work. Those iterations had different bases, different records and different brands, and voters met them as separate governments rather than as one long incumbent.

It isn't a claim about party continuity so much as about the province's centre of gravity: how often the government of the day sat to the right of centre over the post-war period. As a summary of frequency rather than of lineage, the aggregate still tells you something about the odds a premier is weighing.

items.title: B.C.'s Election Call, Weighed Against Six Decades of the Right and 22 Years of the NDP
items.body: British Columbia Premier David Eby's decision to call a provincial election a full two years before the next scheduled vote is a strategic gamble, and the province's own political arithmetic is part of what makes it a plausible one to take now rather than later. As The Conversation Canada frames it, Eby has bet the future of his NDP government on re-election being easier in the current climate than in 2028 — the reasoning the author draws from the long history of B.C.'s party system, which he describes as a recurring polarization between left and right, with the left carried first by the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation and then by the NDP, and the right passing through several successive iterations over the decades. His own calculation puts the shape of that history in numbers: about six decades of post-Second World War government by the various parties of the right in British Columbia, against just about 22 years in power for the NDP. Read that way, an early vote is a bet on timing — a governing party choosing to face voters inside a stretch when it believes it can win, rather than waiting for the province's usual pattern to reassert itself. The count is the author's, and the outcome is a separate question from whether the bet was a rational one.

sources.title: The Paris Auto Show is full of interesting cars Americans can’t have

items.title: Paris Delivered a Full Auto-Show Debut Day, With a Warning for U.S. Readers
items.body: Ars Technica's report from Paris describes a show behaving the way auto shows used to: its media day, held the day before the report, produced debuts aplenty — framed as a step back into the era when automakers rolled out new cars at the event itself. The author also tells you what the piece is for. It is meant to irritate you, he says, because he is pretty sure none of what he saw will come to the United States. That makes the revival a strange sort of good news: evidence the trade-show format still works, presented as a window display for the readers least likely to be able to order from it.

sources.title: Hurricane Simon Lurks Off the Mexican Coast

items.title: Hurricane Simon Passed as a Category 4, and the Sierra Madre Took Some of the Edge Off
items.body: Hurricane Simon passed close to Mexico's Pacific coast as a category 4 storm on October 11, 2026, the latest in what NASA's Earth Observatory describes as a long progression of tropical cyclones in the Eastern Pacific that season. The National Hurricane Center noted that the topography of the Sierra Madre mountains appeared to temper the storm's intensity somewhat and shrink the size of its wind field. Notice the hedging: 'appeared to temper', 'somewhat'. The note doesn't claim the mountains broke the storm — it credits them with taking some of the edge off, a smaller and more interesting claim about how much of a hurricane's strength actually reaches the coast.

sources.title: Google wants to host your personal vibe-coded apps in the Play Store

items.title: Ask Play Started as a Chatbot on Store Listings. Now It's a Way to Search the Store
items.body: Google rolled out Ask Play in 2025 as a small chatbot interface on Play Store listings — something to interrogate the app you were already reading about. Per Ars Technica, it is expanding into a more general way to search for apps and games, with users asking questions and the system generating recommendations that can include detailed comparison charts; Gemini is due to roll out a similar capability soon. The chat layer is not the interesting part. A comparison chart is an argument about which app wins rather than a longer list of candidates, which changes what a store search is for: not retrieval but a recommendation with reasons attached. Whether that beats a ranked list for the person choosing between five near-identical apps is an open, testable question.

sources.title: APOD: 2026 October 14 – Mars and the Beehive Under an Aurora

items.title: An Aurora, a Solar Eruption, and Mars in the Beehive
items.body: NASA's Astronomy Picture of the Day for October 14 shows Mars inside the Beehive cluster — M44, also called Praesepe — beneath a curtain of aurora, above a horizon near Lansjärv, Sweden. The caption calls it a cosmic coincidence, and the geometry is only half of it. The other half is what made the light in the first place, and it is not the Sun glowing at us directly. An eruption off the Sun reached Earth on October 10, 2026, causing strong disturbances in Earth's magnetic field. The colours are a conversion process: energetic particles from that eruption energize molecules in the atmosphere, and those molecules then release the extra energy as light. Nothing burns. The bright curtain is Earth's own air, briefly excited — with Mars parked inside the Beehive cluster in the same frame.

sources.title: Mixture-of-Experts kernel engineering on Amazon SageMaker AI

items.title: What Fusing Actually Does for a Mixture-of-Experts Model
items.body: A Mixture-of-Experts model is a sparsely activated architecture: it scales a large language model's capacity while keeping the compute spent per token low. Serving one well is largely a kernel problem, and the technique AWS describes is fusion. A fused MoE system merges token routing, data shuffling and the specialized network calculations into a single batched operation on the GPU. That buys latency, and it charges for it: the same write-up flags added complexity in kernel implementation and debugging, plus the hardware-specific tuning required to get high GPU utilization. So “sparse” describes the mathematics, not the engineering. The architecture saves compute per token; collecting that saving inside a running service is careful, machine-specific work. And since this is AWS describing its own optimization, the performance framing is the vendor's own.

sources.title: Saudi conflict with Houthis escalates with new strikes
Saudi Arabia's military struggle against Houthi attacks

items.title: Saudi Airstrikes on Yemen's Oil Facilities, and Houthi Attacks That Keep Coming
items.body: PBS NewsHour reports that the Saudi-led coalition launched new airstrikes on oil facilities across Houthi-controlled Yemen, in response to deadly airport attacks in Riyadh. Houthi rebels in Yemen are again targeting Saudi infrastructure and military sites, an escalation PBS says may yet draw in other regional powers. Deutsche Welle describes the same exchange from the Saudi side, reporting that Houthi attacks on airports and energy facilities are putting the kingdom under pressure. Two things sit together here: the coalition is hitting back hard, and the strikes it is answering keep arriving. That combination is what makes the prospect of wider involvement something other than hypothetical.

sources.title: Is it OK for jobseekers or employers to use AI?

discussion.body: The pressure is positional, not moral. When the people you're up against are using the same tools, restraint looks like a handicap you chose for yourself.
'No choice' is still an overstatement. There is a choice — it's just an expensive one, and expensive choices are precisely the kind a hiring market should be thinking about.
Then the race continues, because the cost lands on the individual while the benefit of fixing it lands on everyone.

items.title: Graduates, AI Applications, and the Logic of 'No Choice'
items.body: BBC reports that graduates are increasingly using AI to misrepresent themselves in job applications, according to research, and that some of them say their peer group has no choice. The second half is the interesting half. It is a positional argument rather than a moral one: if enough of the people you are competing against are using the same tools, restraint stops looking like integrity and starts looking like a handicap you volunteered for. That does not make the embellishment honest, and it does not make the trend and the rationale the same kind of claim — one is measured, the other is how people describe themselves. But it does move the interesting question off graduate character and onto a hiring process that now has to tell the difference between a candidate and a candidate's tooling.

sources.title: Manage private pricing offers for Amazon Bedrock with managed entitlements

discussion.body: The unwelcome version of this bug doesn't break the pipeline. The model still answers; it just answers at a price nobody negotiated.

Switching a grant on everywhere the moment a contract exists isn't obviously right either. The problem isn't that the default is off — it's that the off state is invisible to everyone except the invoice.

items.title: The AWS Setting Where a Negotiated AI Rate Quietly Doesn't Apply
items.body: AWS Marketplace Private Pricing Offers exist so an organisation can negotiate custom rates for third-party models on Amazon Bedrock. AWS's own guidance flags the step that decides whether those rates ever take effect: in an AWS Organization with all features enabled, organisation-level grants are auto-accepted but stay Disabled until someone activates them — and until someone does, the negotiated pricing does not apply. Accepted, but not in effect. The contract is agreed, the grant exists, and the meter runs on the old terms. Activating by hand works, AWS notes, but it adds effort and is easy to miss. That is the shape of failure worth remembering in AI procurement: nothing crashes, no error surfaces, and the only symptom is likely to appear as a number on an invoice. Accepted and applied are separate states, and nothing in the workload will flag the difference.

sources.title: Trump Accounts expand to millions of children, but new rules raise questions

discussion.body: The missing veto is the striking part. A child's account can end up holding a single company's shares chosen by someone else, and the household has no way to decline.
A five-year lock-up is at least a legible rule — no churn, no quick flip. Pairing five years of no exit with no say over the asset is the combination that's hard to justify.

items.title: Trump Accounts Auto-Enrolled 60 Million-Plus Children; Donated Stock Comes With Strings
items.body: The Treasury Department has created Trump Accounts for every eligible child, automatically enrolling more than 60 million of them, PBS NewsHour reports. The expansion also came with changes to how the program works. The rule worth noticing: donors can now give individual stocks, and families cannot choose or reject them — and the shares must be kept for five years. An account holding one company's stock, picked by whoever made the donation and locked in for half a decade, is a different instrument from a plain savings pot. Whether that turns out to be generous or risky depends on what ends up in the account, which is precisely the part the family doesn't control. PBS's Amna Nawaz discussed the changes with Wall Street Journal reporter Richard Rubin.

sources.title: Prime Minister Carney to attend 2 Forever Canadian rallies in Alberta ahead of Oct. 19 referendum

items.title: Carney Adds Two Alberta Rallies Before the Oct. 19 Referendum
items.body: Prime Minister Mark Carney says he has accepted an invitation to attend two Forever Canadian rallies in Alberta this week, ahead of the Oct. 19 referendum. CBC reports he will make a stop in Calgary on Thursday and another in Edmonton on Friday. A sitting prime minister giving two consecutive days to one province in the closing stretch of a referendum campaign is a scheduling choice that reads as a position, and it is harder to soften later than a statement from Ottawa would have been.

sources.title: BAFTA Winner Narges Rashidi Signs With TFC Management

items.title: 'Prisoner 951' BAFTA Winner Narges Rashidi Signs With TFC Management
items.body: Narges Rashidi, who recently won the BAFTA for Leading Actress for her portrayal of Nazanin Zaghari Ratcliffe in the BBC's Prisoner 951, has signed with TFC Management, Deadline reports. The series, directed by Phillipa Lowthorpe and also starring Joseph Fiennes, is described by Deadline as telling the true story of Zaghari Ratcliffe's wrongful seven-year imprisonment in Iran. An agency signing is normally the least interesting sentence a trade outlet can print. Here the award behind it is the heavier fact: a leading performance built on a real imprisonment, in a drama that braided a family's ordeal into television.

sources.title: New York Times Op-Docs Acquires ‘The Revolution Against Death,’ Oscar Nominee Joshua Oppenheimer’s Film On Quest For Immortality

discussion.body: A festival named the Revolution Against Aging and Death gets shortened to The Revolution Against Death for the film — half the promise is gone before the opening credits.
Or the film is pointed at the harder half. Aging is a process you can argue with; death is the deadline you can't.

items.title: A Short Film Set at a Longevity Festival Lands at NYT Op-Docs
items.body: The New York Times' Op-Docs platform has acquired The Revolution Against Death, a short directed by two-time Oscar nominee Joshua Oppenheimer, Deadline reports. The documentary is set at an annual longevity conference called the Revolution Against Aging and Death Festival, and NYT Op-Docs and MUBI will co-release it globally in early December. The title compression does a lot of thematic work: the festival promises a revolution against aging and death, and the film keeps only the second half of the target.

sources.title: 3rd-party advertisers can’t appoint scrutineers in Alberta referendum and both sides aren’t happy about it

discussion.body: When federalists and separatists object to the same ruling, neither can claim the referee is working for the other side. Around this referendum, that may be as close to consensus as it gets.
Shared annoyance isn't agreement about anything except the annoyance. Both camps may simply dislike losing an option they assumed they had.

items.title: Alberta: Third-Party Advertisers Can't Appoint Scrutineers, and Both Camps Are Unhappy
items.body: Elections Alberta has told registered third-party advertisers that they will not be able to appoint scrutineers in the upcoming referendum — a decision CBC reports has drawn criticism from campaigners on both the federalist and separatist sides. That both camps are unhappy is the interesting part. A procedural ruling that irritates both sides equally is either a sign of even-handedness or of a rule cutting against something each side assumed it had, and either reading says the campaign is being fought over the machinery of the vote as much as the question on the ballot.

sources.title: Ukraine and the US: What's next after Trump's diesel deal with Russia?

items.title: Trump Plans to Let Russian Diesel Be Purchased, and Objections Come From Two Directions
items.body: Donald Trump plans to allow the purchase of Russian diesel, Deutsche Welle reports, a decision that has drawn criticism at home and abroad. DW says it has taken the questions of what lies behind the move, and what Ukraine should do next, to experts. Criticism arriving from two directions at once is the detail that lingers.

sources.title: Cornell University bans frat parties, vows to address 'disturbing' campus culture

items.title: Cornell's President Apologizes to a Student Who Alleges Rape at a Fraternity House
items.body: NPR reports that Cornell's president sent a letter apologizing for what happened to the student who alleges she was raped by several men at a fraternity house in 2024, and promising 'meaningful action.' The letter attaches an institutional acknowledgment to an allegation dated 2024. The promise is the part that can be measured later.

sources.title: Quebec flu vaccine appointments open amid warnings of early flu season

items.title: Quebec opens flu vaccine appointments as officials warn of an early season
items.body: Quebec's health and social services department has opened flu vaccine appointments, and it is telling vulnerable people to get their shots before the holiday season rather than wait for the usual late-autumn window. The department also notes that only some vulnerable people will receive the shots free of charge.

sources.title: Vancouver Film Festival Audience Award Winners: ’I Play Rocky,’ ‘Ceremony’ Among Big Wins

items.title: Peter Farrelly's 'I Play Rocky' takes the top audience prize at VIFF
items.body: Peter Farrelly's film about the making of *Rocky* — the underdog story of how Sylvester Stallone got the movie made and ended up starring in it — has won the Audience Award in the Galas & Special Presentations category at the 2026 Vancouver International Film Festival. It was one of ten titles audiences picked as favourites across the festival's programming.

sources.title: BondIt, Buffalo 8 and Sandaled Kid Productions Team Up on High-Concept Horror Film Slate (EXCLUSIVE)

items.title: BondIt, Buffalo 8 and Sandaled Kid plan a three-film horror slate
items.body: BondIt Media Capital, Buffalo 8 Distribution and Sandaled Kid Productions have partnered on a slate of three commercial, high-concept horror films. BondIt is financing; Buffalo 8 is handling release; Sandaled Kid is leading development and production. The pitch, at least as announced, is volume and concept rather than a single auteur-driven project.

sources.title: Bank of America hit with $1.2bn fine for money laundering failings

items.title: Bank of America fined $1.2bn over money-laundering failings
items.body: The US Treasury has fined Bank of America $1.2bn, saying the bank inadequately flagged transactions linked to potential Chinese money-laundering networks. That is the specific failure named in the Treasury's account, and it is the reason the penalty lands on a bank rather than on the networks themselves: the compliance system is the thing under examination. A fine of this size is not a reprimand about paperwork. It prices a control function that regulators judge to have missed the transactions passing through it.
